INTRODUCTIONM
As the world's population increases so too does the demand placed on an already overcrowded RF spectrum.
AM communication systems (such as CB) work with a significantly reduced bandwidth reflecting the more limited range of the human voice. This conserves space within the spectrum.
Still, much of the space available for communication radio is taken up by AM systems such as CB, shortwave, etc. Therefore, narrowband FM communications was the next logical step.
Today, emergency services such as police, fire departments, ambulance services and cordless telephones commonly use narrowband FM radio.
Like its AM counter-part, the primary advantage of NBFM is RF spectrum conservation.
NBFM is also a popular communications format with the U.S. Military. During hours of darkness, AM signals are prone to bouncing outside of their assigned range.

In a battlefield situation, this could have disastrous results if troop locations were inadvertently revealed to the enemy. Further, FM is inherently less noisy; reducing the risk of misunderstood information and commands.

DISCUSSION
In Amplitude Modulation, amplitude is the modulating component in the signal and frequency remains constant.
In Frequency Modulation, amplitude is constant while frequency is modulated. That is, the "intelligence" is carried in minute, instantaneous variations in the frequency.
While the above is the obvious difference between AM and FM, there are many others benefits and deficits between the two forms of modulation. Some are more apparent than other.

We know that in AM there are only three frequencies; the carrier and the first two sidebands. Frequency modulation presents an entirely different picture mathematically because it has the carrier and the upper and lower sidebands.
For example, when a frequency modulated signal is derived from a 5 kHz modulating frequency, the resultant frequency will have sidebands at 5 kHz intervals to infinity.
The sidebands, as they progress outward in either direction from the carrier, will continually become weaker and weaker; but, none-the-less, are still present.

Those sidebands that contain the majority of the power are considered significant sidebands. This, of course, makes FM a far more complex form of modulation than AM. It also is the factor that indicates the need for some sort of limiting device.
FM sidebands have equal amplitudes and are always an equal distance from the carrier frequency. This keeps FM sideband distribution in a symmetrical format around the carrier frequency.
1. When a carrier frequency is modulated, its power is reduced.
2. Any energy removed from the carrier is added to the sidebands.
3. The greater the amplitude of the modulating signal, the more power produced in the sidebands.
4. In frequency modulated signals, the sidebands may contain more power than the carrier.

NBFM communications systems operate exactly as broadcast FM, except for the narrower operating band. The modulation still consists of frequency variations in the carrier, there are still guardbands, and so on.
Like AM communications, voice is the primary intelligence being processed; removing the necessity of a broader frequency range.
So, while broadcast FM occupies a 200 kHz bandwidth, narrowband is reduced to, typically, 10 kHz to 30 kHz.

The heart of the Nida NBFM Transmitter (PC130-456) is the Motorola 2833 low power FM transmitter subsystem. Throughout the lesson the schematics may be viewed by entering <Ctrl-S>.
This one IC encompasses nearly an entire FM transmitter. It includes an RF oscillator, variable reactance network, buffer, microphone amplifier and two auxiliary transistors.
It is referred to as a subsystem because it still requires external components to make it work. These components include a crystal oscillator, tuning section, power supply, filters and so on.
Prior to examining the inner workings of the IC, we will first take a look at the PLL and tuning section.

The Nida NBFM tuner is Phase Locked Loop based and uses a quad dip switch package for channel selection. Despite the 16 possible switch combinations, the PLL chip's decoder only allows for 10 individual channels..
This particular chip defaults to channel ten for any input combination (dip switch) whose binary value is above 10.
Hence, a binary 12 on the transmitter's dip switch will still call up channel 10 (49.970 mHz) in the PLL's on-board ROM look-up table.

The chip was designed for multiple uses and in this application will tune to the top 10 upper channels assigned for low power narrow band FM frequency allocation. Applications include cordless phones, baby monitors, and walkie-talkies.

The PLL chip is fully duplexed. This means that it is capable of simultaneous transmit and receive operations; just like your telephone.
However, the Nida card set utilizes this chip in a simplex configuration, where transmit and receive functions must be processed separately, as is the case with most all radio communications.
The IC is capable of locking two different voltage controlled oscillators at the same time on two different frequencies to allow duplex operation in applications like cordless phones.
Since our application is for training and is simplex (one channel) only, the output of Phase Detector 1 at Pin 13 of the IC is unused. d. This is, as the schematic is labeled, PD1.

The reference oscillator frequency is internally divided by 2048 to produce a 5 kHz reference signal, viewable using the oscilloscope or frequency counter. This is handy for confirming operation of the reference oscillator.

The output of the reference oscillator, 10.24 MHz, is also available at TPB1. A X10 probe must be used for viewing the signal to prevent circuit loading. The recommended confirmation of the reference oscillator is the divided 5 kHz clock at TPB4.
The Mode select switch, S1 on both the PC130-456 and the
PC 130-457 is a chip option from the cordless telephone application made switch-selectable for training to assist with alignment and troubleshooting.
S1 selects either the "Base" or "Handset" mode. The U2 internal divide-by rate differs between the two modes with the handset mode transmitting frequency about 3 MHz higher than the base mode.

The switches must be set in the opposite position between the transmitter and the receiver. The system will not work with both switches in the same position as the receiver tuned frequency will be about 3 MHz above or below the transmitter frequency.

Channel selection is done with S3, a DIP switch with 4 toggle switches providing a BCD input to U2 at Pins 5 through 8. Although allowing 16 different selections, "0000" and all selections above "1010" are ignored...
Active HIGH, the channel select BCD chosen at S3 can be confirmed at D0 through D3, available at TPB 5, 6, and 8.

FI1 (pin 14) and FI2 (pin 9) are the inputs to the divide by N counters for the receive and transmit sections. In the configuration for this system, pin 14 is not being used because PC130-456 is the transmitter.

U2 Pin 10 is the "phase locked" output. 4.5 VDC is an unlocked condition, and 4.25 VDC is a locked condition. This is an active LOW output but it drops to only 4.25 VDC on the transmitter since only one of the two phase detectors is used in the PLL circuit...

The VCO output signal is divided and compared to a reference signal to produce the phase lock steering signal that leaves U2, Pin11 and is cleaned by a low-pass filter network before being applied to the VCO circuit in U1.

When sound enters the microphone, it is converted to AF and routed to pin 5, U1. The amplifier's output is at pin 4 which is a feedback line through variable resistor, R5, back to the audio input at pin 5.
Audio from the microphone or the external source enters U1 Pin 5 and exits at Pin 4 after being amplified. The audio enters U1 again at Pin 3 and is applied to the variable reactance circuit.

The output of the Variable Reactance circuit is the modulation audio which leaves Pin 1 and is applied to the oscillator circuit at Pin 16 through C30. The audio modulates the frequency of the oscillator, thus RF FM is generated...
From pin 14, the FM signal passes through a tank circuit made up by C8, C22 and L2. It then travels through C14 to the base of Q2 at pin13 where it is amplified and sent to the collector at
The signal then passes through another tank circuit consisting of L3 and C16 on its way to the base of Q1 for further amplification.
Upon leaving the transistor at pin 9 (the collector of Q1) the cleaned and amplified signal passes through yet another tank circuit consisting of L4 and C12, on its way to the antenna.
The output of the final tank can be measured at TP6. From there the signal is processed for impedance matching by use of C18 and C9 and then sent to the antenna for transmission.
As with the transmitter, the receiver of the Nida NBFM communications system is contained on a single IC, the MC13135.

A block diagram of the receiver, even though contained mostly in a single IC, shows a standard dual-conversion FM receiver. Those receiver functions outside the single IC are inside the dotted lines.perational amplifier.

The Pin numbers for the receiver IC, U1, have been added to the block diagram. U2 performs as the audio amplifier. U3 is the PLL circuit and provides both local oscillator frequencies to the receiver...

The difference signal leaves the mixer at Pin 18 and is applied to X2, a 10.7 MHz ceramic bandpass filter. The filtered signal then re-enters U1 at Pin 20 and is applied to the 2nd Mixer.
The other input to the 2nd Mixer is the PLL primary clock output of 10.245 MHz. The difference signal, this time 455 kHz

X1 is another ceramic bandpass filter, but this time with a resonant center frequency of 455 kHz. The output of the filter is applied to the input of the Limiter at Pin 9.
The connection between the output of the Limiter and the input of the Demodulator is internal to U1. The Quadrature Coil has a single connection in the circuit, Pin 13.
The demodulated audio goes through 1 stage of amplification before leaving U1 at Pin 17.
The audio signal is applied to R7, the Volume Control, and then U2, the Audio Amplifier. Amplified audio is then channeled to the speaker.he discriminator.
The Phase Lock Loop circuitry is a standard PLL circuit. A clock signal of 10.245 MHz is divided 2048 times to produce a reference clock of 5 kHz.
The VCO output is divided a set number of times based upon the channel selected and then compared to the 5 kHz reference clock.
The divided frequency from the VCO should be 5 kHz. The PLL circuit adjusts the DC voltage to the VCO so the sampled output of the VCO equals the 5 kHz reference clock in both frequency and phase...
When the frequency and phase of the two signals agree the system is "locked".t is at pin 16 which is used to bias Q1 which drives the Channel Detect LED.
The frequency of the on-board clock oscillator is 10.245 MHz, is a popular frequency for PLL clocks. It can be divided by a common factor, 2048, to produce a 5 kHz reference clock.

The 10.245 MHz frequency is also useful in dual-conversion receivers as it is the exact difference between the two IF frequencies, 10.7 MHz and 455 kHz, and can be directly applied to the 2nd Mixer...
The remaining parts of the PLL circuit are common to the transmitter PLL circuit on the PC130-456 card. Channel selection is done using S2. Ten channels can be selected..

The "Base" and "Handset" modes are selected using S1. The frequency difference is roughly 3 MHz between the two. When in the "Handset" mode the receiver is tuned to receive the lower frequencies than the "Base" mode.
TPB1 provides the necessary test points for trouble shooting the PLL circuit. The 10.245 MHz clock is available at Pin 1.tions as it is primarily designed for use with a cordless telephone.
Pin 2 at TPB1 has the Phase Detect feed to Local Oscillator 1 in U1. The votage at this point will be between 1.2 and 3.5 volts DC dependant upon the mode, channel, and lock condition.
TPB1 has the Mode condition on Pin 3, HIGH in the Base mode, and LOW in the Handset mode. Pin 4 has the 5 kHz reference clock availabel, a 5 Vp-p square wave.o the 1st IF.
Finally, the channel state can be determined at Pins 5 through 8. "0001 through "1010" are valid selections. Out of range selections are set to channel 1, "0001".al entering the first mixer.
